data.seasonDescription: Use extra caution on this trail in the winter. The trail follows the stream very closely in places, so snowy conditions can cover up the stream, causing hikers to step into the water by accident.
data.accessibilityInformation: This unpaved, natural surface trail has steep grades for the first half mile. The trail then narrows significantly and follows a stream through a marshy area. Service animals are permitted.
data.feeDescription: As of January 1, 2025, a park entrance fee is required to enter Valles Caldera National Preserve.
data.locationDescription: The Jemez River Trailhead is a locked cable gate at a gravel two-track road on the west side of the main entrance road, about 1/2 mile from the entrance gate. Please do not block the gate; park beside the entrance road. No backcountry pass required.
data.longDescription:
This 3.4-mile (5.5 km) out-and-back trail features breathtaking views along the East Fork Jemez River as it flows toward the southwestern corner of the preserve. The trail initially climbs up a hill with outstanding views of Valle Grande and then drops down into the canyon of the East Fork. From here, you'll hike downstream, passing volcanic rock formations along the way. Some parts of the trail may be marshy.

Use extra caution on this trail in the winter. The trail follows the stream very closely in places, so snowy conditions can cover up the stream, causing hikers to step into the water by accident.

Elevation: 8,406 - 8,573 feet

data.title: Hike the Cerro La Jara Loop
data.shortDescription: The Cerro La Jara Loop is a gentle, 1.4-mile hike around Valles Caldera's smallest and youngest volcanic dome. The hike takes approximately 1 hour. Leashed pets are permitted.

images.altText: Two leashed dogs walk side-by-side in front of us on a narrow trail in a large grassland valley
images.title: Hiking La Jara Trail
images.caption: Roxy and Zuma, two leashed dogs, walk side-by-side on the Cerro La Jara Loop.

data.seasonDescription: This is one of the few hiking trails that is accessible year-round at Valles Caldera National Preserve.
data.accessibilityInformation: This unpaved, natural surface trail is approximately 18 inches wide. Over 1.5 miles, the elevation range is between 8497 and 8545 feet.
data.timeOfDayDescription: Valles Caldera National Preserve is open to vehicular traffic from 9 AM to 5 PM during the winter season and 8 AM to 6 PM during the summer season. Pedestrian traffic can access the park and its trails from dawn to dusk every day.
data.feeDescription: As of January 1, 2025, a park entrance fee is required to enter Valles Caldera National Preserve.
data.activityDescription: This is an easy, relatively flat loop hike that circles Cerro La Jara, a small volcanic dome that formed about 500,000 years ago. It is a narrow, unpaved trail. Sections of it, particularly on the southwest side of Cerro La Jara, can get marshy, so prepare to get your feet wet if hiking after the spring thaw or during monsoon season.
data.locationDescription: Park at the Welcome Station. Cerro La Jara Loop begins at the sign between the Welcome Station and the solar panels.
data.longDescription:
This 1.5-mile (2.4 km) loop trail circles Cerro La Jara, the smallest volcanic dome in the park, which formed about 500,000 years ago when lava oozed up and onto the caldera floor. South Mountain, to the west, and Cerro del Medio, on the opposite side of Valle Grande, are also volcanic domes and can be seen from this trail.

The trail passes through a prairie dog colony; they'll be keeping an eye out for you and will make an alarm call as you approach and then scurry underground. Keep an eye out for them (and their large burrows) and their main predator, the coyote. Elk may be present late in the day at the base of South Mountain. There will be a good crop of wildflowers along the trail during the summer monsoon season.

Elevation: 8,497 - 8,545 feet
data.durationDescription: This loop hike takes visitors an average of one hour to complete.

data.title: See the Angus Show Cattle
data.shortDescription: A black Angus cattle herd still pasture in the fields once grazed by Eisenhower's own show herd. Visitors to the Eisenhower farm were often treated to a farm tour complete with Eisenhower showing off his pride and joy, the show cattle and show barn.

images.altText: A closeup of a cow looking directly at the camera with a silo in the background.
images.title: The Angus Cattle are Sure to Amuse You
images.caption: Cattle at the Eisenhower farm are seen and herd!

data.location: The Show Barn at Eisenhower National Historic Site
data.accessibilityInformation: The pathway to the show barn is a several hundred yards at a slight grade and a gravel road, so it may be difficult for persons with mobility issues or those who use a wheelchair.
data.longDescription:
A short walk from the Eisenhower Home, visitors can see exterior of the Show Barn where Eisenhower's black Angus cattle were pampered and prepped for farm shows. Along the route visitors will see the various farm buildings and silos that date from the 19th and early 20th century. The 1957 Show Barn reflects Eisenhower's desire to apply the best available science and technology to farming.

During his presidency Eisenhower used his farm as a diplomatic tool. World leaders like Prime Minister Nehru of India, Sir Winston Churchill, and Soviet Premier Nikita Khrushchev toured the farm and the Show Barn.

 Check the park website for hours and directions.

Although the original line of Eisenhower's herd was all sold off near the end of Ike's life, the National Park Service leases the field to local farmers who maintain an Angus cattle herd.

data.title: Bunsen Peak Road Ski Trail
data.shortDescription: The Bunsen Peak Road Ski Trail is a one-way skier-tracked easiest to most-difficult trail with two trailhead options. This ski affords views of Swan Lake Flats, the Gardner Canyon, and the Gallatin Mountains.

images.altText: Two skiers travel across a flat meadow with mountains in the distance.
images.title: Bunsen Peak Road Ski Trail

data.accessibilityInformation: This skier-tracked trail follows a mostly flat dirt road for the first three miles when accessed from the trailhead on Swan Lake Flats. The section accessed from the YCC Camp is most difficult due to icy curves and steep downhill sections. Total elevation gain/loss for the trail is 1120 feet. Service dogs allowed with backcountry access permit.
data.petsDescription: Qualified service animals are welcome throughout the park and in all park facilities. However, they must be leashed and under your control at all times. This trail requires a backcountry access pass for service animals.
data.feeDescription: No fees are required, however, one-way or round-trip skier shuttles may be offered for this trail.
data.activityDescription: Easiest to most difficult.
data.locationDescription: The trail can be accessed from the Mammoth-Norris Road, just south of Rustic Falls and across from the upper end of the Snow Pass Ski Trail at Swan Lake Flats. The other trailhead is located within the Youth Conservation Corps (YCC) Camp area from a plowed road in an employee housing area 0.8 miles (1.3 km) below the Upper Terrace parking area and 1.3 miles (2.1 km) above Mammoth.
data.longDescription:
The Bunsen Peak Road Ski Trail is a 6-mile (9.6-km) one-way, occassionally groomed, easiest to most-difficult trail with two trailhead options. The easier of the two options requires a snow coach drop-off. This trailhead begins from the Mammoth-Norris road, just south of Rustic Falls and across from the upper end of the Snow Pass Trail at Swan Lake Flats. The upper 3 miles (4.8 km) are mostly level and suitable for all levels of skiing ability. On the northeast side of Bunsen Peak, the road becomes steep and winding, dropping 960 feet in 2.5 miles (292 m in 4 km) to Glen Creek. The trail ends at the trailhead located within the Youth Conservation Corps (YCC) Camp area (see below). Return the way you came if you have not arranged a shuttle.

The more difficult option for this trail starts from the trailhead located within the Youth Conservation Corps (YCC) Camp area, from a plowed road in an employee housing area 0.8 miles (1.3 km) below the Upper Terrace parking area and 1.3 miles (2.1 km) above Mammoth. Ski the trail in the opposite direction from the description above, returning the way you came.

Notes: CAUTION: Some curves have steep drop-offs and can be hazardous when icy. Bison and elk frequent this trail. Federal regulations require you to stay at least 100 yards (91 m) away from bears and wolves, and at least 25 yards (23 m) away from bison and all other wild animals.

Check out the ski trail details and accessibility information at the bottom of this page.
data.reservationDescription: Skier shuttle reservations may be required to access this trail. Reservations and information are available at park hotels and at:: 307-344-7311, Toll-free: 866-439-7375, TDD: 304-344-5395.
data.durationDescription: The duration will vary depending on fitness level, snow conditions, and length of time spent along the trail.

data.title: Snow Pass Ski Trail
data.shortDescription: The Snow Pass Ski Trail is a 4.2 mile (6.76 km), skier-tracked, one-way, easiest to most-difficult, ski that takes skiers through a steep heavily forested area to a semi-flat wide open area with views of Swan Lake Flats.

images.altText: Skiers follow a straight trail through a snowy forest.
images.title: Snow Pass Ski Trail

data.accessibilityInformation: This skier-tracked trail provides fairly level terrain for the first 2.2 miles (3.5 km) when accessed from the Glen Creek Trailhead on Swan Lake Flats. The section accessed from the Upper Terrace Loop Ski Trail and Mammoth-Norris Road is most difficult due to icy curves and steep downhill sections when traveled from the Glen Creek Trail toward the Upper Terrace Loop Ski Trail or the Mammoth-Norris Road trailheads. Total elevation gain/loss for the trail is 700 feet. Service dogs allowed with backcountry access permit.
data.petsDescription: Qualified service animals are welcome throughout the park and in all park facilities. However, they must be leashed and under your control at all times. This trail requires a backcountry access permit for service animals.
data.feeDescription: No fees are required, however, one-way or round-trip skier shuttles may be offered for this trail.
data.activityDescription: Easiest to most-difficult
data.locationDescription: Trailheads include one on Swan Lake Flats at Glen Creek Trailhead, a spur from the Upper Terrace Loop Ski Trail, and south of the Upper Terrace Loop Ski Trail parking area from the Mammoth-Norris Road.
data.longDescription:
The Snow Pass Ski Trail is a 4.2-mile (6.76-km), skier-tracked easiest to most difficult one-way ski that takes skiers through a heavily forested area to wide open views of Swan Lake Flats. To get to the Snow Pass Ski Trail take the short connector trail that joins from the upper end of the Upper Terrace Loop Ski Trail. The heavily forested trail ascends 700 feet in 1.5 miles (213 m in 2.4 km) through a series of very steep grades along the trail to Snow Pass. From Snow Pass, the trail continues 0.5 miles (0.8 km) down over rolling terrain to a trail junction where the ski route turns left (south) and follows Glen Creek over fairly level terrain for 2.2 miles (3.5 km), meeting the road just south of Rustic Falls (in the winter, the road is only open to limted travel in oversnow vehicles). From here, you can either continue across the road to the Bunsen Peak Road Ski Trail (see decription) or return the way you came.

Notes: CAUTION: some curves have steep drop-offs and can be hazardous when icy. Bison and elk frequent this trail. Federal regulations require you to stay at least 100 yards (91 m) away from bears and wolves, and at least 25 yards (23 m) away from bison and all other wild animals.

Check out the ski trail details and accessibility information at the bottom of this page.

data.title: Visit Old Slater Mill National Historic Landmark
data.shortDescription: The birthplace of the American Industrial Revolution, Old Slater Mill is open as a museum. Visitors can learn about the history of the site through exhibits, films, and tours. The grounds are open from dawn to dusk. Visitors can read interpretative panels spread across the grounds which help tell the story of the site. Check out the Park's calendar for operating hours and seasons.

images.altText: River in foreground with yellow mill and other buildings in distance
images.title: Slater Mill Campus
images.caption: Slater Mill Campus

relatedParks.fullName: Blackstone River Valley National Historical Park
relatedParks.name: Blackstone River Valley

data.seasonDescription: The mill is open on a seasonal basis. During the winter months (January - March), the mill is closed to the public. Operating hours and seasons vary during the Spring, Summer, and Fall. Check out the Park's calendar of events for up-to-date information about park offerings at the site.
data.accessibilityInformation: The mill is fully accessible to individuals with mobility difficulty. However, the structure is a old textile mill. The floors are at times uneven and the space could be difficult to navigate with a wheelchair. The front door is handicap accessible, but the belltower door is not. Individuals requiring a handicapped accessible door should enter through the front door.
data.ageDescription: This site is good for all ages.
data.activityDescription: Exhibits, introductory video, guided tours, and activities available.
data.locationDescription: Located just off of Roosevelt Avenue, this location offers a large parking lot.
data.longDescription:
Come visit the first industrial building in the United States of America. Slater Mill, first constructed in 1793, was a water-powered cotton spinning mill financed by the Brown family of Providence. Samuel Slater, an English immigrant, working with local mechanics, successfully replicated English textile machines here in the United States in 1790. The wooden mill, now named Old Slater Mill, houses a visitor contact station with exhibits. Tours are also offered of the mill by Park Rangers. Operating hours and tours vary by season. Please check the Park's calendar for the latest information.

The site is also home to the Wilkinson Mill and Sylvanus Brown House. At this time, both of these facilities are closed to the public.

The grounds surrounding these three historic buildings are open daily from dawn to dusk. Interpretive panels spread across the grounds, help to explain the site's history and importance. 

Things to Do:

Visitor Information Station

Watch an 8-minute video, learn more about the Park, or earn your Junior Ranger badge. Park staff are available to answer questions. Bathrooms and drinking water are available.
The Visitor Contact Station is located inside of Old Slater Mill.

Guided Tours: 
Join a Ranger for a tour of Old Slater Mill. These 30 - 45 minute programs talk about the the legacy of the Industrial Revolution in America's first cotton-spinning mill. Tours leave from the patio in front of Old Slater Mill.
The mill is accessible but does have uneven floors. Special accommodations can be made by contacting 401-725-8638.

Spring Schedule (April 24, 2025 - May 16, 2025)

Visitor Information Station: Open Fridays and Saturdays (10:00 A.M. - 4:00 P.M.)

Guided Tours: Fridays and Saturday (10:30 A.M., 12:30 P.M., 2:30 P.M.)

Park Grounds: Open Daily (Dawn - Dusk)
 

Summer Schedule (May 17 - October 31)

Visitor Information Station: Open Thursdays - Sundays (10:00 A.M. - 4:00 P.M.)

Guided Tours: Thursdays - Sundays (10:30 A.M., 12:30 P.M., 2:30 P.M.)

Park Grounds: Open Daily (Dawn - Dusk)
 

Fall Schedule (November 1 - November 28)

Visitor Information Station: Open Fridays and Saturdays

Guided Tours: Fridays and Saturdays (10:30 A.M., 12:30 P.M., 2:30 P.M.)

Park Grounds: Open Daily (Dawn - Dusk)
 

For visitor safety, tours of Old Slater Mill will be modified or canceled if the heat index is above 87 degrees Fahrenheit. A shortened 10 minute Ranger talk will be offered at the normal tour times. Visitors will have a brief period of access to the main part of the mill. For the latest weather information, call 401-725-8638.

 

Please Note: The Wilkinson Mill and the Sylvanus Brown House are currently closed to the public until critical accessibility and safety work is completed. Due to this, group tours are required to be smaller than those offered in the past.

If you are looking to book a special group tour of Old Slater Mill or are a teacher or student check out our education page for more information.
data.durationDescription: Depending on how much time you have and whether or not you go on a guided tour will dictate how long you will spend at the site. Visitors just interested in collecting a stamp, reading through indoor and outdoor exhibits should allow 15 - 30 minutes. If going on a guided tour, tours last around 30 minutes.

data.title: Hiking with Traction Devices
data.shortDescription: Enjoy the winter wonderland that Rocky has to offer from late October to early June. When there is hard-packed snow and ice on the trails, don't forget to use traction devices!

images.altText: A person is hiking on a snow-covered trail with traction devices
images.title: Hiking in winter with traction devices
images.caption: Hiking in winter & spring with traction devices

data.accessibilityInformation:
During the winter and spring seasons, from late October to early June, expect conditions on trails to vary.

Factors like elevation and access to direct sunlight have an impact on the amount of snow or ice that might be on a trail. During the winter and spring seasons, most trails in Rocky Mountain National Park are covered with snow and ice.

Traction devices are helpful when hiking on hard-packed snow and ice. For soft and deeper snow, it is best to switch to snowshoes.
data.petsDescription: Pets are not allowed on any trails in Rocky Mountain National Park.
data.activityDescription:
Enjoy the winter wonderland that Rocky has to offer from late October to early June. When there is hard-packed snow and ice on the trails, don't forget to carry and use traction devices!

Traction devices help prevent slips and falls when walking on snow and ice. There are many different types of traction devices available. They attact to the bottom of your boots and provide extra grip for the soles of your boots.

Along with traction devices, remember to wear layers of warm clothing and waterproof boots. Hiking poles are also helpful when hiking year-round.

Activity is available for families.

In this new activity designed especially for families, visitors explore Old North through a scavenger hunt narrated by Prince, the friendly North End cat who used to frequent the church. By finding clues and answering questions, participants will see highlights of the sanctuary and learn about Old North’s unique history. 

This activity is included with your admission ticket! To participate, simply request a copy of Prince’s Pew Pursuit when you enter the church.

For more information, visit Old North Church's website.

data.title: Old North Church: Crypt Tour
data.shortDescription: Take a self-guided tour of Old North’s historic crypt, where 1,100 people were laid to rest.

images.altText: Inside a small red-brick crypt with a shelf that has a couple boxes and a coffin shaped box.
images.title: Old North Church Crypt Tour
images.caption: "See What Lies Beneath Old North"

data.accessibilityInformation: Participants should be comfortable in a basement setting and navigating tight spaces. The crypt has low lighting, uneven surfaces, and is not wheelchair or stroller accessible.
data.feeDescription:
Visitors may purchase the Crypt Combo package during normal operating hours. The Crypt Combo is $9 per person when you book online, or $10 at the ticket booth. It includes a self-guided tour of the crypt, general admission to the church’s sanctuary and new exhibit, and an immersive audio guide with 300 years of the church’s secrets and stories. Children 5 and under are free.

Visit Old North's online schedule to plan your visit.
data.activityDescription: Note: Participants should be comfortable in a basement setting and navigating tight spaces. The crypt has low lighting, uneven surfaces, and is not wheelchair or stroller accessible.
data.longDescription:
Did you know that over 1,100 bodies lie underneath the sanctuary of Old North Church? Explore Old North’s crypt on a self-guided tour. You’ll find out about the burial practices of early congregants, get introduced to some of the notable crypt "occupants" who have rested in this unique space for hundreds of years, and learn about discoveries from recent archeological work.

Content: Historical topics discussed include death, burials, and human remains.

Note: Participants should be comfortable in a basement setting and navigating tight spaces. The crypt has low lighting, uneven surfaces, and is not wheelchair or stroller accessible.

For more information, visit Old North Church's website.
data.reservationDescription: Reservations are not required, but it is possible to reserve tickets in advance. Please visit Old North Church's Admission & Pricing page for more information.
